items.title: Houston Person Part 2 interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, October 2, 1998 [interview 2 of 2]
items.q: So if you go back and listen to those 78’s, that Charlie Parker and Dizzy and Miles did, you’ll see that their solos were short and they did it all.

ctx.x: Do you find that that’s something that you feel the jazz audience needs these days? To have a musician keep the songs perhaps a little shorter so that you don’t alienate anybody?

Well not necessarily. I think that if you don’t have anything to say for so long and trying to get it together on stage, I don’t go there. You should know what you’re going to say when you get up there and get it over with. So if you go back and listen to those 78’s, that Charlie Parker and Dizzy and Miles did, you’ll see that their solos were short and they did it all. I mean those things are amazing. And you try to play some of those solos, transcribe them, and you can’t. And they were the ones that were…

That’s a great point. And it’s interesting how the technology has allowed other things to happen but perhaps not all that positive. I mean you have — to do a CD now, you’re expected to do almost an hour of music.
